01 / Snapshot

The case in one minute.

Project creation was fragmented: users had no clear sequence from starting a project to reaching its dashboard.

I led the wider redSling redesign across research, journey mapping, information architecture and developer handoff. This case study focuses on the project-creation journey: grouping related setup, distinguishing essential from optional details, and making progress visible.

02 / Problem + stakes

Creating a project had no clear path.

The previous experience did not guide users step by step from project setup to the dashboard.

Related information lived across separate flows. Users had to leave creation, find another area, and work out what still needed to be completed. The interface gave little indication of how much setup remained.

01 — NO GUIDANCE

The next step was unclear

There was no structured sequence showing what was needed before a project could begin.

02 — FRAGMENTED SETUP

Related tasks lived apart

Users had to jump between areas to finish parts of the same project setup.

03 — LOW VISIBILITY

Progress was hard to judge

It was difficult to tell what was complete, what remained, and what could wait.

03 / My role + reality

I redesigned project creation as one guided journey.

As the UX / Product Designer, I mapped the journey, structured the information, designed the interactions and prepared the flow for developer handoff.

I organised essential information into clear steps and made some setup details skippable so users could reach the dashboard without being blocked by information they might not have yet.

04 / Insight → decision

Guided, but not restrictive.

The design keeps related setup in one place and separates what must be done now from what can be finished later.

01. Make the journey visible

I introduced clear steps so users could understand where they were and what came next.

02. Keep project setup together

I brought related information into one flow, reducing the need to leave creation and search elsewhere.

03. Allow safe deferral

Optional details could be skipped and completed after the core project was created.

04. Reinforce completion

Short supporting text and progress cues help explain each step and show what remains.

The trade-off

Letting users defer non-essential details removes an early blocker, but creates follow-up work. The flow needs to make those unfinished details easy to find later.

05 / Experience

From “where do I begin?” to a ready project.

A visible sequence connects the essential details to the dashboard, while optional work can be completed later.

01 — START
Essential details

Begin with the information needed to create the project.

02 — CONFIGURE
Guided setup

Keep related tasks together and show which steps are optional.

03 — CONTINUE
Project dashboard

Move into the project, with skipped details available to finish later.

06 / Delivery + system

Carrying the logic through to delivery.

The handoff needed to preserve the flow’s behaviour, not just its appearance.

I prepared the redesigned experience for developer handoff as part of the wider redSling redesign. Required and optional steps, progress cues, supporting guidance and the route into the dashboard all needed to remain consistent.

07 / Outcome

A clearer flow was designed. Its impact is still to be measured.

The documented output is the guided project-creation journey and its handoff. I do not yet have verified post-launch or usability results for this flow.

Task successCan users create a project and reach its dashboard without searching elsewhere?
Time and frictionHow long does setup take, and where do users pause or backtrack?
Follow-upCan users find and complete the optional details they deferred?
08 / Learning + next move

Structure should make work feel lighter.

A step-by-step flow helps only if it reduces uncertainty without adding unnecessary work. I would test the minimum path to the dashboard and check whether deferred details remain easy to find afterward.

  • Keep related setup in one journey
  • Make required and optional work explicit
  • Test the return path for skipped details
09 / Trade-offs

Structure without blocking progress.

The guided flow made setup easier to follow, but each simplification carried a cost to consider.

01 — STEPS VS SPEED

A clearer path adds screens

Breaking setup into steps gives users orientation, but can feel slower than one long form. The flow keeps each step focused so progress remains visible.

02 — ONE PLACE VS COMPLEXITY

Consolidation needs hierarchy

Keeping related setup together reduces jumping between areas, but puts more choices in one journey. Grouping information and brief supporting text help prevent overload.

03 — FLEXIBILITY VS COMPLETENESS

Skipping creates follow-up work

Deferring non-essential details gets users to the dashboard sooner, but leaves an incomplete project to revisit. Which details are safe to defer needs validation with the team and users.
